name: Black Blue
lede: Black Blue is a near-black with a cold blue cast, a paint-card name whose root is the old trade term blue black: soot, charcoal and ink that lean blue.

sections.title: Which Black Blue
sections.body:
The swatch is #1D1F2A, a color so dark that it only just reads as blue [1]. The name comes from the RAL paint system, where Black Blue is number 5004, and the earliest record of it in our sources is the 1927 RAL list [1]. RAL colors are printed paint chips, so the on-screen value is an approximation [1].

Our library also pairs the name with the Japanese *kachi-iro*, glossed as a coarse wool color [1]. That pairing is a library mapping, and none of our books discusses it, so treat it as a loose neighbor and not as a translation [1].

sections.title: Black with a touch of blue
sections.body:
Long before paint cards, *blue black* was a pigment word. Paterson's dictionary defines it as black with a touch of blue, and also lists it as a kind of carbon black, cross-referred to Frankfort black [2]. The *Pigment Compendium* says it was more than a qualified color word: it seems to have meant charcoal, named for the blue cast the charcoal has, and a term in general use in the second half of the seventeenth century and after [3]. In the later nineteenth century it could also mean ivory black with a little blue pigment added [3].

Lamp black is the usual blue-black. Coles calls it a lightfast, opaque blue-black pigment that the ancient Egyptians used for tomb painting more than 4,000 years ago, and says the Romans made a version from burnt wine dregs, the best wines giving a black as blue as indigo [4]. Watercolorists later made the same effect on the palette: Gurney describes Payne's gray as a blue-black blended from black and ultramarine or similar mixes [5]. St Clair credits a landscape painter working in Devon with first mixing a deep blue-black grey, which suited the haze of distant hills [6].

sections.title: Ink and cloth
sections.body:
Blue-black is the color of old writing ink. St Clair describes the recipe: tannic acid from oak galls, combined with iron sulfate, water and gum arabic, gives a velvety blue-black ink that is also very permanent [7]. She adds that Theophilus recorded a variant in the twelfth century that used the tannic acid in crushed buckthorn sap [7].

Cloth could be blue-black too. Balfour-Paul notes that the many dippings needed to bring indigo-dyed cloth to a dark blue-black tied it to wealth and religious standing [8]. In Qing China, according to Finlay, pure blue was the official color of minor princes, while blue-black silk marked a civil servant [9]. Our swatch is darker than a dyer's [[indigo]] or a [[navy]] coat; its nearer neighbors are [[bluish-black]] and [[gunmetal]] [1].

sections.title: Bluish black in the mineral lists
sections.body: Eighteenth-century mineralogists needed words for the many near-blacks of rocks. Werner's system used eight principal colors, each modified by a mixture word such as bluish black or greenish yellow [10]. Syme's black series, as Baty tabulates it, runs through iron-black, velvet-black, pitch-black, raven-black and bluish-black [11]. When Jameson issued his third edition in 1817, he added two blues taken from Lenz, blackish-blue and duck-blue [12].

sections.title: Where black meets blue
sections.body:
In medieval heraldry, black (sable) and blue (azure) belonged to the same group of colors. Heraldry sorted its six colors into two groups: white and yellow in one, and red, black, blue and green in the other [13]. The rule forbade placing two colors of the same group side by side or one on the other, except for small details [13]. A black shield could therefore carry a white or yellow lion but not a blue one, so a black-and-blue combination was avoided on arms [13].

Jarman uses black-blue as a mood [14]. Looking at Geertgen's *Nativity at Night*, he writes of a black blue sadness in which the virginal blue robe is swallowed by black [14]. It is a personal reading, not a documented painters' term [14].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 1,014 (4.3 per cent) have a patch within six units of this color (CIEDE2000) covering at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [15]. The match is most often a shadow: in 99 per cent of those paintings it sits at the dark end of the picture's own lightness range [15]. It peaks in the 1930s, with 6 of 69 paintings (8.7 per cent), about twice the museums' baseline [15].

The painter who uses it most often is [[painter:gustave-caillebotte|Caillebotte]], with 6 of his 22 works in the archive, 6.4 times the baseline [15]. The strongest single match is [[painting:commons-Q21725392|Snack]], a Dutch painting of 1650 in which this near-black covers 87 per cent of the canvas, which says more about the dark, varnished picture than about any pigment [15]. The earliest match is an ostracon with a drawing of a king, dated about 1295 BCE, which is a look-alike in an aged photograph and no evidence of a pigment [15]. In printed English the two-word phrase peaks around 1921, though it also counts the words side by side, as in black, blue [15].

All of these numbers are for museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings. A color match is not a pigment test, and dark values vary most with photography [15].

questions.q: In old pigment language, what was blue black?
choices: Black with a touch of blue, such as charcoal or lamp black
A mix of indigo and Prussian blue
A color invented by RAL in 1927
questions.answer: Black with a touch of blue, such as charcoal or lamp black

questions.q: Why was a black shield with a blue lion avoided in medieval heraldry?
choices: Black and blue belonged to the same color group, which could not touch
The lion had to be white
questions.answer: Black and blue belonged to the same color group, which could not touch
